summaries.example: Imagine a game with a set of toy blocks. The language has names such as "red," "blue," and "on top of," plus rules for combining them. A structure is one actual arrangement of blocks that gives meaning to those names and relations. Two arrangements may look different but still make every sentence in the language true or false in the same way. They are then elementarily equivalent.
summaries.summary: First-order model theory is a part of mathematics about descriptions and the objects that satisfy them. A first-order language contains symbols for names, properties, relations, and functions. A structure is a collection of objects that gives those symbols meanings. We can ask whether a sentence is true in a structure and compare structures by the sentences they satisfy. The entry explains several kinds of maps between structures. An embedding preserves the basic facts, while an elementary embedding preserves every first-order fact. It also introduces major theorems. The compactness theorem says that if every finite group of rules can be satisfied, then the whole group can be satisfied. The Löwenheim–Skolem theorems show that structures can often have elementary versions of different sizes. Other constructions make products, ultraproducts, saturated structures, and models containing special indistinguishable sequences. Finally, the entry describes research programmes that look for orderly families of models, geometric patterns, and tame behavior in ordered structures.
key_ideas: First-order model theory studies the connection between formal descriptions and the structures that satisfy them.
A language supplies symbols; a structure gives those symbols meanings.
Different structures can agree on every sentence in a language even when they are not the very same structure.
Elementary maps preserve all statements expressible in the language.
Important results show how to build smaller or larger structures with the same first-order behavior.
The subject helps mathematicians study algebra, geometry, computation, and other areas.
summaries.why_it_matters: Model theory gives mathematicians a way to compare rules with the worlds in which those rules hold. It can reveal when a description is too weak to choose just one structure, or when many structures share the same first-order behavior. Its ideas have been used in algebra, geometry, the study of real numbers, computer science, and questions connected with machine learning. It also teaches a broad lesson: changing the language can change what a structure looks like and what can be proved about it.

important_terms.definition: A carefully chosen collection of symbols and rules for making statements about things.
A domain of objects together with meanings for the language's names, properties, relations, and functions.
A sentence or group of sentences that is true in a structure.
When two structures make exactly the same sentences in a language true.
A map between structures that preserves the meanings of the symbols in the required way.
A map that preserves all first-order statements, not just the simplest ones.

questions_to_think_about: Can two different-looking things obey exactly the same set of rules?
What might a language fail to describe?
Why could it be useful to make a larger structure that still agrees with a smaller one?
How is copying a structure different from merely making a similar-looking copy?

summaries.example: Consider the language of groups, with a constant for the identity and a binary operation for addition. The integers and the even integers can be related by the map n ↦ 2n. This is an embedding because addition is preserved, but it is not elementary: in the integers, 1 is not twice another integer, while 2 is twice 1. Thus preserving the basic operation does not guarantee preservation of every first-order property.
summaries.summary: First-order model theory investigates how formal theories relate to their models. A signature supplies constants, relation symbols, and function symbols; formulas are built from these together with logical operations and quantifiers. An interpretation of the signature produces a structure, and Tarski's truth definition determines which formulas hold there. The complete theory of a structure is the set of all its true sentences. Structures that are isomorphic are equivalent in a particularly strong structural sense, whereas elementary equivalence means only that they satisfy the same sentences in the selected language. The entry then studies homomorphisms, embeddings, and elementary embeddings. This distinction matters because an embedding may preserve atomic information while failing to preserve quantified properties. Model-complete theories make every embedding between models elementary, while quantifier elimination gives an even stronger simplification of formulas. The compactness theorem, diagram lemma, interpolation, omitting types, and the initial model theorem form a group of central results. Products, ultraproducts, saturation, and Ehrenfeucht–Mostowski constructions provide ways to build new models. The final sections describe categoricity and classification theory, geometric model theory, and o-minimality, including links with algebra, geometry, number theory, and some areas of theoretical computer science and machine learning.
key_ideas: Model theory separates syntax—the formal descriptions—from semantics—the structures that make descriptions true.
Isomorphic structures are structurally identical, while elementarily equivalent structures need only agree on all sentences in the chosen language.
The choice of signature matters: adding function or relation symbols can change generated substructures and what is expressible.
Compactness and the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems show that first-order theories often have models of unexpectedly different sizes.
Quantifier elimination replaces formulas by simpler equivalent formulas; model-completeness only guarantees elementary behavior of embeddings.
Major research programmes study categoricity, classification, geometric dependence, and o-minimal or 'tame' ordered structures.
summaries.why_it_matters: First-order model theory clarifies what a formal theory can and cannot determine. Compactness explains why finite consistency can lead to a full model, while the Löwenheim–Skolem results show that first-order descriptions of infinite structures commonly allow models of several cardinalities. These facts shape debates about categoricity and about whether a theory captures one intended mathematical object. The subject also provides reusable constructions and structural dividing lines. In applications, such methods help identify theories whose models have manageable patterns, connect algebraic and geometric behavior, and transfer logical insights into other mathematical settings.

important_terms.definition: A formal language built from a signature and logical symbols, allowing quantification over individual objects but not over sets or properties.
A domain together with interpretations of the language's constants, relations, and functions.
A structure in which every sentence of a theory is true.
The set of all first-order sentences true in a structure.
A map preserving atomic statements; with equality included, an embedding is one-to-one.
An embedding preserving the truth of every formula, including formulas with quantifiers.
The principle that a theory has a model if every finite part of it has a model.
A theory is model-complete when every embedding between its models is elementary; this is related to, but weaker than, quantifier elimination.

questions_to_think_about: Why can two nonisomorphic structures agree on every sentence of a particular first-order language?
What does the upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem suggest about first-order theories with infinite models?
Why is quantifier elimination a stronger property than model-completeness?
How might adding a new symbol to a language change the substructure generated by the same element?
When is a classification of models informative rather than merely a list?

summaries.example: Suppose a school club uses a small rule language: it can name members, say who is friends with whom, and describe operations such as pairing members. One actual club arrangement is a structure because the symbols receive meanings there. Another arrangement might have different members but make every sentence in the language come out the same way. The two arrangements are elementarily equivalent. A map between them may preserve simple friendship and pairing facts, yet fail to preserve a statement such as "there is a member with a certain property." An elementary map must preserve both kinds of statements.
summaries.summary: First-order model theory studies the relationship between formal descriptions and the structures that make those descriptions true. A signature contains symbols for objects, relations, and functions. From it we build a first-order language, and a structure interprets the symbols over a domain. Truth is then defined inside that structure. This makes it possible to compare structures. Isomorphic structures are essentially the same after renaming their elements, but elementarily equivalent structures merely agree on every sentence expressible in the language. Maps also come in levels: homomorphisms preserve basic structure, embeddings preserve atomic information in both directions, and elementary maps preserve all formulas. The entry explains how elementary substructures and extensions fit together. It presents four results about them, including the downward and upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorems, which produce elementary structures of controlled sizes. Five central theorems include compactness, which turns finite satisfiability into full satisfiability, and interpolation, which can provide a sentence using shared vocabulary to separate incompatible theories. Other sections discuss ultraproducts, saturation, and indiscernible sequences. The entry ends with three broad programmes: classification of models, geometric analysis of definable dependence, and o-minimality, which studies ordered structures whose definable sets have especially controlled shapes.
key_ideas: Model theory compares formal rules with the structures that realize them.
The same structure can be viewed differently when the language or signature changes.
Elementary equivalence is weaker than being isomorphic: agreement about sentences does not necessarily give a one-to-one structural match.
Elementary embeddings preserve more information than ordinary embeddings.
First-order theorems can create elementary substructures and extensions with selected sizes.
Researchers study when theories have orderly models and when their models become too varied for a simple classification.
summaries.why_it_matters: Model theory helps us ask precise questions about the power of mathematical language. A theory may describe many possible structures rather than one unique object, and its models may vary in size or complexity. The main theorems explain some of that variation and provide methods for constructing useful examples. The subject matters beyond logic because its ideas connect with algebraic fields, groups, geometry, the real numbers, computer science, and newer work related to learning theory. It also shows why definitions and choice of vocabulary can strongly affect mathematical conclusions.

important_terms.definition: A formal system of symbols for talking about individual objects, their properties, relations, and functions.
A collection of objects that interprets every symbol in a first-order language.
A structure that satisfies all the sentences in a theory.
Two structures are elementarily equivalent when they satisfy exactly the same sentences in a chosen language.
A structure or theory containing another while preserving the original interpretations of its symbols.
A map that preserves every formula, including statements involving 'there exists' and 'for every.'
A theory has quantifier elimination when every formula has an equivalent quantifier-free description within the theory.
A theory has a model if each finite collection of its sentences has a model.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a language be unable to tell two different structures apart?
What extra information is preserved by an elementary map?
How does compactness connect finite sets of rules with an infinite set of rules?
Why could mathematicians want both small elementary substructures and large elementary extensions?
What might make a theory 'tame' rather than highly unpredictable?
